chapters.title: Chapter 3: Behavioral Economics in Pricing, Business, and Negotiation

lessons.title: Decoy Pricing and Choice Overload: Lessons from Swiggy, Zomato, and Streaming Plans

children.text: A streaming app shows three plans: Mobile at ₹149, Standard at ₹499, Premium at ₹649. Mobile feels too limited, Premium feels needlessly expensive for features you probably won't use, so Standard, sitting right in the middle, feels like the obviously sensible choice. Almost nobody stops to ask why the plans are priced and positioned exactly this way. They are, and the answer has very little to do with what streaming actually costs to deliver.

body.text: Adding a third, deliberately unattractive option to a choice between two things can shift which of the original two people pick, without changing either of them at all. The extra option isn't there to be chosen. It's there to make one of the real options look better by comparison.

children.text: The Decoy Effect: Ariely's Economist Experiment

markDefs.definition: A pricing tactic where a third option is added to a choice set specifically because it is clearly worse than one of the existing options, in order to make that option look more attractive by comparison. Also called asymmetric dominance.

children.text: Behavioral economist Dan Ariely ran the demonstration that made the

famous, using real subscription options from The Economist magazine. He offered participants a web-only subscription at $59, a print-only subscription at $125, and a print-plus-web subscription also at $125. The print-only option is a decoy: nobody would rationally pick it over the identical-priced print-plus-web option, which offers everything print does, plus more, for the same money.

body.caption: What one useless option did to everyone else's choice

cells: Decoy removed, only two options shown

body.text: The print-only decoy was chosen by essentially nobody, yet its mere presence on the page flipped the majority choice from web-only to print-plus-web, the more expensive option. A decoy doesn't need to sell. It only needs to make a neighbouring option look like an obviously better deal by comparison.

markDefs.definition: The tendency to favor a middle option that sits between a clearly stripped-down cheap option and a clearly expensive premium option, because the middle choice feels like a safe, moderate compromise. Distinct from the decoy effect, since the middle option is genuinely comparable to both extremes rather than clearly dominated by one.

children.text: The streaming app's three tiers use a close cousin of the decoy effect called the

, described by marketing researcher Itamar Simonson in 1989. Unlike a decoy, which is clearly dominated by one specific option, a compromise-effect middle tier is a genuine choice, just one made to feel like the moderate, low-risk option purely by virtue of sitting between two extremes. Very often, the middle tier is exactly the one the business most wants sold: priced to be profitable, positioned to look neither cheap nor indulgent, flanked deliberately by a stripped-down option and a premium option that exist mainly to make the middle one look right.
Swiggy and Zomato: Decoys on the Menu, Not Just the Plan

Food delivery menus run the same play at a smaller scale. A burger alone is ₹149. Fries alone are ₹99. A cola alone is ₹49. A burger-fries-cola combo is ₹219, positioned right next to all three, doing the arithmetic for you: buying separately would cost ₹297, so the combo saves ₹78. Almost nobody orders fries or cola alone at those standalone prices. That's not a pricing failure, it is the standalone prices doing their real job, which is making the combo look like the obviously smart choice, exactly like the Economist's print-only decoy.

body.title: Price the combo's real margin
body.prompt: The restaurant's actual cost to make the burger, fries, and cola together is ₹100. At the ₹219 combo price, what is the restaurant's profit margin over cost, as a percentage?
body.explanation: Profit = ₹219 − ₹100 = ₹119. Margin over cost = ₹119 ÷ ₹100 = 119%. The combo genuinely does save the customer money compared to the inflated standalone prices, and it is still a highly profitable order for the restaurant. Those two facts are not in tension, they are the entire design.

children.text: Choice Overload: When More Options Backfires

markDefs.definition: The finding that too many available options can reduce, rather than increase, the likelihood of a satisfying decision or a decision at all, by making comparison overwhelming rather than easier.

children.text: Decoys and tiers work by narrowing choice, but too much genuine choice creates its own separate problem:

. Sheena Iyengar and Mark Lepper's widely cited 2000 study set up tasting booths in a grocery store: one displaying 24 varieties of jam, another displaying just 6. The 24-jam booth drew more browsers, but only around 3% of them actually bought a jar. The 6-jam booth drew fewer browsers, but roughly 30% of them bought one, a tenfold difference in purchase rate from showing fewer options. More choice attracted attention. It did not attract decisions.

body.text: Later research, including a 2010 meta-analysis by Alexander Chernev and colleagues, found choice overload is real but not universal: the effect shows up most strongly when options are hard to compare, the chooser has no clear prior preference, or there's no obvious default to fall back on. Don't treat "more options are always worse" as a fixed law. Treat it as a specific failure mode worth designing around.

children.text: This is exactly why Swiggy and Zomato, sitting on catalogues of thousands of restaurants and menu items each, lean so heavily on curated shortcuts: "Bestsellers near you," "Trending," "Rated 4.3 and above." These aren't neutral information displays. They are a direct countermeasure to choice overload, a simplification nudge from Chapter 1, applied at the exact moment a hungry, time-pressed user would otherwise be facing thousands of unranked options and the satisficing behavior from Chapter 1's bounded rationality lesson.

body.title: Decoy, compromise, or overload?
body.question: A software company sells a Basic plan at $10/month, a Pro plan at $49/month, and a Business plan at $50/month with far more features than Pro. Almost everyone picks Business. What is the $49 Pro plan most likely functioning as?
options: A genuine compromise option, chosen by moderate users
A decoy, priced almost identically to a clearly superior option specifically to make Business look like the obvious deal
Evidence of choice overload reducing conversions
An anchor with no other function
body.explanation: When one option is priced almost the same as another but offers unambiguously less, and gets chosen by almost nobody, that is a decoy doing exactly its job, pushing choice toward Business, the same pattern as the Economist's print-only subscription.

body.title: Redesigning a pricing page
body.scenario: A SaaS founder shows you her pricing page: Starter at ₹999/month with core features, and Pro at ₹4,999/month with everything, including features most customers don't need. Conversion to Pro is low, and many prospects simply leave without buying either plan.
body.prompt: Using the concepts from this lesson, what would you suggest she test, and why?
body.modelAnswer:
1. With only two options far apart in price, there's no compromise-effect middle tier to make Pro feel like a safe, moderate choice, and no decoy making either option look like the obviously smart pick, buyers are left comparing two very different products with no anchor to judge them against.
2. A worthwhile test is adding a genuine middle tier, priced and featured between Starter and Pro, which the compromise effect suggests could draw hesitant buyers who currently abandon the decision entirely rather than pick either extreme.
3. Separately, if there's a specific plan she wants to push, she could test a near-priced decoy just below it, clearly weaker on one dimension, mirroring the Economist and streaming-app examples.
4. She should also check whether prospects are leaving from overload rather than pricing alone. If the page lists too many granular feature comparisons without a clear "most customers pick this" cue, a simplification nudge, similar to Swiggy's "Bestsellers," highlighting a recommended plan, may lift conversion as much as any pricing change.

body.title: Name the effect
body.textWithBlank: Adding a third option that is clearly worse than one of the two real options, specifically to make that option look better by comparison, is called the ___ effect.
body.explanation: The decoy effect, also called asymmetric dominance, is distinct from the compromise effect, where a middle option looks good simply for sitting between two extremes rather than for dominating a specific rival.

body.caption: Three related but distinct pricing effects

cells: A clearly inferior option makes a specific rival option look better by comparison
The Economist's print-only subscription; the Pro plan next to Business
A middle option feels safe simply for sitting between two genuine extremes
The streaming app's Standard tier, between Mobile and Premium
Too many comparable options reduces, rather than increases, decisions made
24-jam versus 6-jam tasting booths; thousands of unranked restaurants on a delivery app

body.title: Did the jam study really prove "more choice makes people unhappy"?

children.text: The original jam study measured purchase conversion, not happiness, and it became one of the most cited findings in behavioral economics, popularized further by Barry Schwartz's book "The Paradox of Choice." But subsequent researchers have not always replicated the effect at the same size, and Chernev's 2010 meta-analysis found it depends heavily on context: how similar the options are, how much expertise the chooser has, and how the options are displayed. The honest, defensible version of this lesson is narrower than "more choice is always bad": it's that an unstructured, hard-to-compare choice set can overwhelm a decision, and curation or defaults are a legitimate design response, not proof that fewer options are inherently better.

body.label: The jam study's purchase-rate gap
body.context: Purchase conversion from Iyengar and Lepper's 24-jam versus 6-jam tasting booths, despite the larger display drawing more initial interest.

cards.definition: Adding a clearly inferior third option to make a specific rival option look better by comparison. Also called asymmetric dominance.
Favoring a middle option because it sits between two genuine extremes, described by Itamar Simonson in 1989.
The finding that too many comparable options can reduce, rather than increase, satisfying decisions or decisions made at all.
Deliberately pricing and positioning items on a menu or pricing page to steer customers toward a specific, usually more profitable, choice.
A simplified, ranked subset of a large catalogue, such as "Bestsellers" or "Trending," used specifically to counter choice overload.

points: The decoy effect shows that adding a clearly inferior third option can flip a majority choice between two other options, even though neither of those two options changed at all.

The compromise effect is a related but distinct pattern: a middle option feels safe simply for sitting between two extremes, which is why three-tier pricing pages so often steer buyers toward the middle tier.

Restaurant combo pricing on apps like Swiggy and Zomato runs the same logic at menu scale: inflated standalone prices exist mainly to make the combo look like the smart choice, while remaining highly profitable either way.

Choice overload shows the opposite failure mode, too many comparable options can reduce decisions and purchases, though later research shows the effect depends heavily on context rather than being a universal law.

Curated shortcuts like "Bestsellers" or a recommended pricing tier are a direct, deliberate response to choice overload, narrowing an unmanageable choice set back down to one a boundedly rational person can actually satisfice on.
